title: Unwritten traditions named — general sense vs viva voce; not in Canonical books
source_text: XI. Atque hae sunt quas vocant traditiones non scriptas, quo nomine intelligunt dogmata & instituta pertinentia ad fidem atque religionem, quae Scripturis canonicis consignata non fuerunt. De quibus, ut quae sit eorum sententia, distinctius intelligatur, sciendum est, fatentibus ipsis Pontificiis, traditionis nomen ex se generale esse, & significare doctrinam omnem quae ab uno traditur & communicatur alteri, sive per scriptum, sive extra Scripturam. Et ita tradere est idem quod docere, & traditio idem quod documentum. Sed tamen usus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum traditionis vocem plerunque restringit ad doctrinam non scriptam, sed viva voce traditam: & ita sumunt hanc vocem Pontificiae Scholae. Neque tamen per doctrinam non scriptam, intelligunt eam quae nullibi scripta est, sed quae scripta non est a primo authore, seu potius, ut eorum quidam accuratius dicunt, quae scripta non invenitur in libris Canonicis Prophetarum & Apostolorum.
pass_a_gloss: And these are what they call unwritten traditions, by which name they understand dogmas and institutes belonging to faith and religion that were not consigned in the canonical Scriptures. So that their view may be understood more distinctly, it must be known — the Pontificians themselves confessing it — that the name tradition is of itself general and signifies every doctrine handed on and communicated from one to another, whether by writing or outside Scripture. And so to hand on is the same as to teach, and tradition the same as a teaching. Yet the usage of ecclesiastical writers for the most part restricts the word tradition to doctrine not written but handed on by living voice: and so the Pontifician schools take this word. Nor by unwritten doctrine do they understand that which is nowhere written, but that which was not written by the first author — or rather, as some of them say more carefully, that which is not found written in the Canonical books of the Prophets and Apostles.
pass_b_english: What they label unwritten traditions are dogmas and religious institutes never lodged in the canonical books.
Even Pontificians grant that tradition as a word is broad: any teaching one person communicates to another, in writing or outside Scripture. Handing on equals teaching; tradition equals a teaching.
Church writers, however, usually narrow the term to teaching given by living voice rather than writing — and that is how the Pontifician schools use it.
They do not mean a doctrine that exists nowhere in writing, but one the first author never wrote — or, more carefully, one absent from the Canonical books of Prophets and Apostles.
